'''''Haemanthus coccineus''''', the '''blood flower''', '''blood lily''' or '''paintbrush lily''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the amaryllis [[family (botany)|family]] Amaryllidaceae, native to [[Southern Africa]]. Growing to {{convert| 35|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall and wide, it is a [[bulb]]ous [[perennial plant|perennial]] with short brown stems surmounted by red flowers, the flowers appearing in spring and summer, before the strap-shaped leaves.<ref name = RHSPF/>

The generic name ''Haemanthus'' is derived from the Greek words ''haima'' for blood and ''anthos'' for flower; ''coccineus'' is the Latin word for red or scarlet. In the [[Afrikaans language]] it is known as '''bergajuin''', '''bloedblom''', and many other vernacular names.<ref name="plantzafrica">[http://www.plantzafrica.com/planthij/haemancoc.htm PlantZAfrica.com] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111029044717/http://www.plantzafrica.com/planthij/haemancoc.htm |date=2011-10-29 }} accessed 11.11.2011</ref>

==Distribution==
''Haemanthus coccineus'' is widespread throughout the winter rainfall region in Southern Africa - from the southern parts of [[Namibia]], to [[South Africa]] in the [[Cape Peninsula]], to the [[Keiskamma River]] in the [[Eastern Cape]].<ref name="plantzafrica"/> It is found in [[Renosterveld]] and [[Fynbos]] [[habitat]]s.

It is an adaptable species, growing in a wide range of soils derived from sandstones, quartzites, granites, shales and limestones. It will survive annual rainfall ranging from {{convert|100|-|1100|mm|in}}. The plant adapts to a wide range of altitudes, being found from coastal dunes to {{convert|1200|m|ft}} high mountains. It is hardy down to about {{convert|1 |C|F|abbr=on}} but does not survive freezing temperatures for any length of time.<ref name = RHSPF/>

It is often found in clumps of hundreds, under the shelter of other shrubs on flat land, or in shady ravines and rock crevices.

[[File:Haemanthus_coccineus.jpg|thumb|125px|right|Flower emerging.]]
[[File:Gardenology-IMG 4993 hunt10mar.jpg|thumb|125px|right|Foliage.]]

==Description==
The flowerheads of ''Haemanthus coccineus'' emerge between February and April{{where|date=November 2023}}, with 6-9 stiff red [[spathe]] valves surrounding 25-100 flowers. The flowers are soon followed by translucent, fleshy berries, white to red in color. There are usually two large leaves per bulb, and occasionally three, which appear after flowering. The leaves are [[Glossary of leaf morphology#elliptic|elliptic]] to broadly shaped, 25–210 mm wide, most often more-or-less barred with red or dark green on the underside; they may also be prostrate, recurved or stand suberect.<ref name="plantzafrica"/>

The brilliant flowerheads account for its early appearance in Europe, being described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1762. Together with ''[[Haemanthus sanguineus]]'' (Jacq.), this was the first ''Haemanthus'' to be introduced to European horticulture as an [[ornamental plant]]. In cultivation in the [[UK]], ''H. coccineus'' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web
| url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/8202/i-Haemanthus-coccineus-i/Details
| title= RHS Plantfinder - ''Haemanthus coccineus''
| accessdate= 3 March 2018
| archive-date= 4 March 2018
| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180304231608/https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/8202/i-Haemanthus-coccineus-i/Details
| url-status= live
}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 45 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 2 March 2018 | archive-date = 5 January 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180105180412/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | url-status = live }}</ref> It can be grown outdoors in a warm, frost-free, sheltered, south-facing location.

Despite Linnaeus' description, this same species was described under a host of different names (see gallery captions), which reflects more on taxonomic disorganisation than species variability. The plant figured on the left, was first described as ''Haemanthus hyalocarpus'' by Jacquin in 1804, and those in the gallery below, which are all ''H. coccineus'', were first described under the caption names.
